Imaging of the Elbow
 CORE
September 24, 2025
Laura E. Stoll, MD
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Determine how standard imaging studies of the elbow are obtained.
Specify special imaging views and sequences used in evaluating pathology about the elbow.
Identify common radiographic abnormalities of the elbow.
Radiography
Radiographs of the elbow include AP, lateral, and oblique views.
Radiographs should be evaluated for joint congruency of the ulnohumeral and radiocapitellar
joints, fractures, joint effusion, and arthritis. In patients with a posttraumatic elbow injury,
overall alignment and the carrying angle of the elbow should be assessed.
Stress views allow for evaluation of the integrity of the medial ulnar collateral ligament (MUCL)
and/or the lateral collateral ligament complex.

For comminuted distal humerus fractures, a traction AP view, in which axial traction is applied
to the extremity, may better define fracture fragments.
The fat pad sign represents an effusion of the joint and suggests an occult fracture.
The drop sign is observed on a lateral view and is concerning for lateral collateral ligament
complex insufficiency.
The double arc sign is indicative of a shear fracture of the capitellum.
The fleck sign is a small cortical avulsion from the olecranon concerning for triceps injury.

Radiography
The anatomy of the elbow is complex, which leads to confusion and difficulty in
interpreting imaging studies. Radiographic views of the elbow include a supinated AP
view, a lateral view with the elbow flexed 90°, and an oblique view1 (Resource 1). An AP
view is obtained with the patient in a sitting position with the elbow extended and the
forearm supinated. The x-ray beam is centered on the elbow and perpendicular to the
cassette. If the patient is unable to fully extend the elbow to obtain an AP view, the
surgeon should obtain two radiographs: one radiograph centered on the humerus (best
demonstrates the distal humerus) and one radiograph centered on the ulna (best
demonstrates the joint and the proximal forearm).
A lateral radiograph is obtained with the patient in a sitting position with the elbow
flexed 90° and the forearm in neutral with the thumb positioned upward. The x-ray
beam is centered on the elbow, almost perpendicular to the cassette and angled 7°
distally. Surgeons must understand the anatomy of the distal humerus to appreciate and
interpret lateral elbow radiographs. The three bony structures that should be positioned
concentrically in obtaining a lateral radiograph include:
The capitellum
The widest portion of the medial lip of the trochlea
The narrowest portion of the trochlear groove
A true lateral radiograph reveals the following findings:

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000038
2/22

The diameter of the trochlear groove is smaller than that of the capitellum.
The medial epicondyle is superimposed over the anterior third of the distal humerus
rather than centered.
Three concentric circles should be observed; the cortex of the trochlear groove is
concentric with and of a smaller diameter than the capitellum and the medial lip of
the trochlea.
The posterior continuation of the lateral condyle from the capitellum is the most
posterior cortex.
Typically, an elbow trauma radiographic series will include a radial head view or an
oblique lateral view. This view is obtained with the patient in a sitting position and with
the elbow in the same position as that for a lateral view. The x-ray beam is centered on
the elbow and angled 45° cephalad. This view demonstrates the radial head without
coronoid overlap.
If an anterior fat pad sign is observed on the lateral view, then an occult fracture should
be suspected, and surgeons should consider more advanced imaging studies. A line
drawn through the center of the radial neck should bisect the center of the capitellum
regardless of the radiographic view. A drop sign is observed if the radial head does not
bisect the center of the capitellum and is suggestive of severe ligament disruption2
(Figure 1; Resource 2).
SEND FEEDBACK

Figure 1 Lateral radiograph of an elbow demonstrates the drop sign with more than 4
mm of ulnohumeral subluxation and posterior radiocapitellar subluxation. (Reproduced
from Cheung E, Nathani A, Tashjian R, Armstrong A, Morrey M: Elbow trauma sequelae:
Instability, stiffness, non-arthroplasty, and arthroplasty options. Instr Course Lect
2019;68:117-140.)
The double arc sign indicates a shear fracture of the capitellum. This is created from the
subchondral bone of the capitellum and the lateral part of the trochlea. The fleck sign is
a small cortical avulsion from the olecranon that often indicates a long and lateral head
triceps rupture3 (Resource 3).
In examining an elbow radiograph for arthritis, osteophytes typically are observed on the
coronoid and olecranon tips, the olecranon fossa, and the anterior distal humeral. Loose
bodies also may be observed. Severe joint destruction with loss of the ulnohumeral and
radiocapitellar joint space and minimal osteophyte formation are suggestive of
inflammatory arthritis.
Surgeons should be aware of three normal variants in assessing lateral radiographs:1
Supracondylar process

A bony, hook-shaped process that may occur at the anterior aspect of the distal
humerus. It may be a source of median nerve entrapment.
Radial tuberosity
This may appear similar to a lytic lesion if the x-ray beam strikes it head on.
Trochlea in skeletally immature patients
It may have several ossification centers that appear fragmented and may be
confused with fractures.
Computed Tomography
CT scans are indicated in patients with complex intra-articular fractures, complex fracture-
dislocations, severe osteoarthritis of the elbow, heterotopic ossification, or proximal
radioulnar synostosis.
Three-dimensional CT reconstructions aid in preoperative planning for complex fractures
about the elbow.

Computed Tomography
CT scans of the elbow typically are obtained with the arm fully extended and the forearm
supinated.1 CT provides better detail of cortical and trabecular structures compared with
MRI but is associated with increased radiation exposure. CT scans often are difficult to
interpret depending on the position of the elbow. Gantry position and reformats must
be in the plane of humerus and the forearm (depending on the pathology) to allow for
adequate interpretation of images.
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction may aid in visualizing fracture fragments.
Subtraction of major bony structures, such as the humerus and ulna, in assessing radial
head fractures may aid in preoperative planning. CT performed with intravenous
contrast may help determine if vascular injury adjacent to the joint is present.
Disadvantages of CT include radiation exposure and limited soft-tissue characterization.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:25 PM

5/22

Metallic implants may cause disruptive image artifact; however, modern, dual-energy CT
data and extrapolation techniques may reduce metal artifact.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Best imaging study for evaluating soft tissues, bone contusions, and osteochondral defects.
Magnetic resonance arthrography is associated with increased sensitivity and specificity with
regard to the detection of ligamentous injuries about the elbow.
In patients with osteochondritis dissecans, magnetic resonance arthrograms aid in assessing
the size of the lesion, the extent of edema, and the status of the cartilage.
A T-sign indicates a partial MUCL tear.
Most chronic overuse tears of the MUCL in overhead throwing athletes occur at the
midsubstance of the ligament.
Because of its orientation, the lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL) typically is not observed
in its entirety on a single coronal MRI.
LUCL tears most commonly occur at the humeral attachment.
Radial head subluxation on sagittal MRIs is a sign of LUCL insufficiency because the radial head
moves with the ulna, creating ulnohumeral incongruency and gapping.
In evaluating for a distal biceps rupture, flexed abducted supinated positioning maybe used.
Patient Positioning and MRI Basics

Patient Positioning and MRI Basics
The patient is placed in the prone or semi-prone position with the arm extended
overhead4 (Resource 4). This allows the elbow to be near the center of the bore of the
MRI scanner. Patients who cannot tolerate such positioning can be placed in the supine
position with the arm at the side.
Stronger magnets provide a higher intrinsic signal-to-noise ratio (eg, a 3 Tesla MRI is
associated with nine times more proton energy than a 1.5 Tesla MRI). In addition, scan
time is decreased with the use of a larger magnet. In T1-weighted MRI sequences, fat
displays a high signal intensity (appears bright). Bone, ligaments, bone marrow, fluid,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:25 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Elbow
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000038
6/22

and fibrocartilage display a low signal intensity (appear dark). T1-weighted MRI
sequences are especially useful in magnetic resonance arthrography. In T2-weighted MRI
sequences, fluid and inflammation display a high signal intensity (appear bright). Bone,
ligaments, muscle, and fibrocartilage display a low signal intensity (appear dark). T2-
weighted MRIs are useful in the evaluation of ligament injuries. Short tau inversion
recovery MRIs are similar to T2-weighted MRIs in that they are fluid-sensitive but afford
more fat suppression, especially in patients with metallic implants. Short tau inversion
recovery MRIs aid in differentiating edema from fatty infiltration. Post-processing
techniques allow for manipulation of data to ensure the best plane of orientation is
used.
Magnetic resonance arthrography aids in the diagnosis of soft-tissue pathology, such as
collateral ligament injuries. Often, magnetic resonance arthrography is not required in
patients with an acute injury because joint effusion that occurs 2 weeks postinjury
creates a native arthrogram. Magnetic resonance arthrography is 92% sensitive and
100% specific for the diagnosis of a MUCL injury5 (Resource 5).
Osteochondral Pathology

Osteochondral Pathology
In patients with Panner disease, or osteochondrosis of the capitellum, the epiphysis
appears as patchy hypointense areas on T1-weighted MRIs. In patients with
osteochondritis dissecans, magnetic resonance arthrograms aid in assessing the size of
the lesion, the extent of edema, and the status of the cartilage. Findings include a rim of
low intensity on T1-weighted images and variable central intensity. Unstable lesions
demonstrate a peripheral ring of increased signal on T2-weighted images with cysts
deep to the fragment. The fragment itself appears hyperintense on T2-weighted images.
Stable lesions demonstrate peripheral low intensity on T2-weighted images that blends
with the normal adjacent bone marrow6 (Figure 2; Resource 6).

Figure 2 Sagittal fluid-sensitive MRI through the radiocapitellar compartment of the
elbow shows an unstable osteochondral fragment (solid arrow) involving the bright
hyaline cartilage and the dark subchondral bone plate. Instability is indicated by cartilage
fissures at the margins of the osteochondral fragment, with a T2-weighted hyperintense
fluid signal tracking along the deep aspect of the lesion. The osteochondral fragment is
on the anterior aspect of the capitellum. A normal pseudodefect of the capitellum is
observed as an irregular area of bone more posteriorly on the capitellum where there is
no overlying cartilage (dashed arrow). (Reproduced from Nacey NC: MRI of the elbow, in
Miller MD, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Sports Medicine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 731-738.)
Medial Ulnar Collateral Ligament

Medial Ulnar Collateral Ligament
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:25 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Elbow
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000038
8/22

The MUCL is composed of three bundles: anterior, posterior, and transverse. The
anterior bundle seen on two to three consecutive coronal MRIs, demonstrating low
signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images. Some regions of higher signal intensity
may be observed at the attachment of the medial epicondyle secondary to fibrofatty
slips. The posterior bundle is fan-shaped and arises more inferiorly from the medial
epicondyle.
Tears are classified as proximal (humeral attachment), mid-substance, or distal (ulnar
attachment). In addition, tears are identified as partial or full A positive T-sign may be
observed if the MUCL appears thin and irregular, especially at the sublime tubercle
attachment, allowing for fluid or contrast below the ligament. However, the MUCL
attachment may thin and become variable in older patients; therefore, this gap may be
normal in older patients. Most tears occur in the mid-substance of the anterior bundle in
patients with a chronic overload injury7 (Resource 7). In evaluating for an acute MUCL
tear, associated findings, such as bone contusions of the lateral compartment and
injuries of the lateral collateral ligament complex, also should be noted.
Lateral Collateral Ligament Complex Structures

Lateral Collateral Ligament Complex Structures
The lateral collateral ligament complex consists of the radial collateral ligament (RCL),
LUCL, accessory collateral ligament, and annular ligament. The LUCL is the only bone-to-
bone attachment along the lateral joint and typically is thought of as the most important
ligament in lateral elbow stability. The LUCL is best observed on coronal MRIs. The LUCL
is completely visible in 80% of patients and is partially visible over its entire course in
18% of patients8 (Resource 8). LUCL failure most commonly occurs at the humeral
attachment (Figure 3).

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000038
9/22

Figure 3 Coronal fluid-sensitive MRI of an elbow shows a tear at the humeral attachment
of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament (solid arrow) with irregular and distally retracted
ligament fibers. The overlying common extensor tendon is thinned, compatible with
partial tearing (dashed arrow). (Reproduced from Nacey NC: MRI of the elbow, in Miller
MD, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Sports Medicine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 731-738.)
In addition to a visible tear, secondary signs of LUCL disruption include radial head
subluxation on sagittal MRIs. Posterolateral translation of the radial head of more than
1.2 mm (sensitivity 67%, specificity 70%) and axial ulnohumeral incongruity of more than
0.7 mm (sensitivity 63%, specificity 70%) are cutoff values that can be used to aid in the
diagnosis of lateral ligament injuries9(Resource 9). Kissing contusions on the posterior
capitellum and the anterior radial head suggest recurrent dislocations.
Tendon Ruptures and Tendinopathies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:25 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Elbow

10/22


Tendon Ruptures and Tendinopathies
Healthy tendons appear as a uniformly low signal intensity on all MRI sequences.
Tendinopathies are associated with areas of thickening with mildly increased
intermediate signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted MRIs. Fluid signal within the tendon
that does not extend beyond the tendon surface indicates intrasubstance tearing. Partial
tears are associated with some loss of tendon fibers. In patients with a chronic tear,
tendon thinning and surface irregularity are observed. In patients with an acute tear,
fluid signal and edema may be observed. In patients with a complete tear, complete
discontinuity of all fibers is observed. Fluid will be observed in the acute phase of injury,
whereas fatty tissue may be observed in the chronic phase of injury. Scarring-in-
continuity also may be observed.
In assessing for a distal biceps tendon rupture, a flexed abducted supinated MRI affords
better visualization of the degree of tendon retraction and allows for better assessment
of partial- versus full-thickness tears (Figures 4 and 5). To obtain a flexed abducted
supinated MRI, the elbow is flexed, the shoulder is abducted, and the forearm is
supinated. In assessing the triceps for tears, surgeons should note that a normal tendon
displays a low/intermediate signal intensity and uniform thickness.

Figure 4 Axial fluid-sensitive MRI of an elbow shows the absence of the normal distal
biceps insertion onto the radial tuberosity (solid arrow) with surrounding edema in the
antecubital fossa, compatible with complete distal biceps rupture. More medially, the
insertion of the brachialis tendon can be seen near the ulnar tuberosity (dashed arrow).
(Reproduced from Nacey NC: MRI of the elbow, in Miller MD, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge
Update: Sports Medicine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic

to echo, 1,000 ms/29 ms) of the right elbow of a 64-year-old man with elbow pain after a
sudden fall and a painful pop in his right elbow shows a full-thickness biceps tendon tear

Typically, lateral epicondylitis involves the extensor carpi radialis brevis (Figure 6). As the
degree of injury increases, concomitant lateral collateral ligament tears may be present.

Figure 6 Coronal, fat-suppressed intermediate-weighted (repetition time/time to echo,
4,000 ms/33 ms; A) and axial, fat-suppressed T2-weighted (repetition time/time to echo,
4,100 ms/63 ms; B) MRIs of the right elbow of a 72-year-old man with elbow pain show a

Asterisk = radial collateral ligament, L = lateral epicondyle, O = olecranon, R = radial

Humeroradial plicae are observed as low signal intensity bands outlined by synovial fluid
or intra-articular contrast. Associated chondromalacia of the anterolateral aspect of the
radial head also may be observed.
Ulnar Nerve

Ulnar Nerve
Normally, the ulnar nerve is flat to oval-shaped and displays a mild signal intensity on T2-
weighted MRIs. In patients with neuropathy, the ulnar nerve thickens and displays an
increased signal intensity on T2-weighted MRIs (Figure 7). An area of 0.08 cm2 has been
suggested as a cutoff value for the diagnosis of ulnar neuropathy10. In patients with an
acute injury, the muscle group supplied by the ulnar nerve may display an abnormally
increased signal intensity on T2-weighted fat-suppressed MRIs.

Figure 7 Axial T1-weighted MRI of an elbow shows striated muscle fibers traversing the
superficial aspect of the cubital tunnel (dashed arrow), consistent with an anconeus
epitrochlearis. The ulnar nerve (solid arrow) lies deep to the anconeus epitrochlearis,
where it can become entrapped, resulting in ulnar neuropathy. (Reproduced from Nacey
NC: MRI of the elbow, in Miller MD, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Sports Medicine, ed
5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 731-738.)
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is most helpful in the evaluation of ligamentous injuries about the elbow and
helps guide injections about the elbow.

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography may aid in the evaluation of superficial soft tissues about the elbow4,11
(Resource 4; Video 1). Medial and lateral epicondylitis will display hypoechoic/anechoic
areas representing focal degeneration. Ultrasonography also has been used to diagnose
acute and chronic biceps and triceps injuries. Ultrasonography can be used to evaluate

joint laxity with dynamic stress and has been used in the assessment of MUCL injuries in
throwing athletes. Ultrasonography also can be used to detect joint effusions and ulnar
nerve abnormalities, aiding in assessment of the size, signal intensity, edema, and
subluxation of the ulnar nerve. In addition, elbow ultrasonography is 96% sensitive and
89% specific with regard to the diagnosis of pediatric elbow fractures.12 Often,
ultrasonography is used to guide intra-articular and peritendinous injections and soft-
tissue biopsies. The diagnostic usefulness of ultrasonography is operator dependent.
Video 1 Rawat M: Introduction, shoulder & elbow, from Patel MR, mod: Musculoskeletal
ultrasound of the extremities: Clinical and ultrasonographic correlation. Presented at the
Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans, LA,
March 6-10, 2018.
Intraoperative Imaging of the Elbow
Intraoperative imaging of the elbow may be cumbersome. In addition, positioning the arm for
intraoperative imaging may torque the elbow, leading to inaccurate radiographic assessment
in patients with instability.
If a posterior approach to the elbow is used, patients can be placed in the lateral decubitus or
prone position, with the C-arm positioned at the head of the surgical table.


Intraoperative Imaging of the Elbow
The patient is placed on a radiolucent cantilever table that is reversed. The down arm
should be in maximum shoulder abduction and elbow flexion, resting on radiolucent
plexiglass. The surgical arm is positioned on a radiolucent arm board in line with the
table axis. Alternatively, plexiglass can be padded with blankets to achieve an
appropriate height. The C-arm is positioned at the head of the surgical table, parallel to
the long axis of the surgical table13 (Figure 8 through 10).

Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2010.)
